RESEARCH NOTE
Gianluca Meola  ·  Research note v0.1  ·  November 2026
Training a Next-Concept Model
on a single 12 GB GPU
Practical gains at small budgets, and a tokenizer gap that remains
Gianluca Meola
gianluca.meola89@gmail.com
20 November 2026  ·  v0.1  ·  Work in progress
Abstract
Next-Concept Models generate text through a hierarchy of discrete codes. I train both the tokenizer and
generator on one RTX 3080 Ti (12 GB), using TinyStories and budgets far below the original paper. Data-based
codebook initialisation lowers generative perplexity by 48% in the tested tokenizer comparison. A retuned
generator recipe lowers it by 56% on the official tokenizer, with most of the gain coming from the learning rate.
Longer tokenizer training helps, but a 1.39× gap to the official tokenizer remains. The study reports reproducible
runs, unsuccessful interventions and limits on causal interpretation.

Evaluation protocol
Each trained generator produces 1,280 unconditional
stories: 256 samples for each sampling seed 42, 0, 1,
2 and 3. Temperature is 1, with no top-k or top-p
truncation. The authors’ evaluation scripts score the
samples with GPT-2 large.
Generative perplexity (Gen. PPL) is the primary
metric. Generated-text entropy must not fall more
than 0.1 below the comparison reference; this guards
against some repetitive outputs. Validation uses the
first 4,096 held-out stories.
Two different kinds of seeds
Training seeds vary initialisation while data order is
fixed. Sampling seeds vary the outputs of one trained
model. Standard deviations across sampling seeds in
the run report are not confidence intervals across
training runs.
Decision rules and scope
Decision rules were written before the corresponding
experiments. Later cycles used 6.7% between single
runs and 4.7% between two-seed means, based on
2.4% training-seed noise measured over five pairs at
51,200 stories. Early cycles used a fixed
five-PPL-point threshold.
These are operational thresholds, not formal
confidence intervals or corrections for a search over
many recipes. Most tokenizers were trained once;
only the longest setting has two tokenizer seeds.
Compute and data exposure
Stories seen count examples processed, including
repeats. Equal exposure does not mean equal optimiser
updates or FLOPs. All results concern TinyStories,
128-token sequences and the tested model sizes; no
larger-language-model distillation is used in this study.

2 The short-budget recipe
A higher learning rate provides most of the measured improvement on the frozen official tokenizer.
Figure 2. Successive changes at 51,200 stories, 400 updates × 128 stories. Bars are means of generator seeds 42 and 43; markers
show individual runs. Percentages are relative to the reconstructed baseline, not the preceding row.
Generator setting
51,200 stories
102,400 stories
Reconstructed paper recipe
Constant corruption + Flex + lr 1e-3
Relative Gen. PPL reduction
What changes
The baseline uses corruption decreasing from 0.75 to
0.25 across levels and lr 3e-4. Constant corruption at
0.5 lowers PPL by 8.5%; adding FlexAttention gives
an 11.7% reduction from baseline. Raising lr to 1e-3
produces the largest change.
The combined recipe retains a substantial gain at
102,400 stories on two generator seeds. Its
performance at the full paper budget is untested.
What this does not isolate
The FlexAttention path omits attention dropout used
by the baseline. Its effect mixes implementation and
regularisation changes. The improvement belongs to
the combined recipe, not to the attention kernel
alone.
Official training code was unavailable in the checked
sources, and the paper omits some training details.
The baseline is a reconstruction, not a verified
reproduction of the authors’ run.
Equal stories do not imply equal optimisation
At the same 51,200 stories, 800 updates × 64 give 83.16 for the baseline, versus 150.67 at 400 × 128. The
alternative has one seed: the 56% result belongs to the stated short-budget comparison.

3 Initialisation, then training
A tokenizer is evaluated by the text generated from its codes, not by reconstruction loss alone.
Tokenizer at 2,400 steps

Perfect stories
L0 codes used
Random codebook initialisation
Initialisation from data (R1)
R1 + early dead-code restart (R12)
PPL means use two generator seeds per frozen tokenizer; each tokenizer has one training seed. Reconstruction and distinct level-0
code counts use 4,096 validation stories. Early restarts stop after step 1,200.
Data initialisation produces the clearest tokenizer gain: −48.2% PPL with the same generator recipe. Early
restart adds −6.2%, but the isolated restart effect still needs a second tokenizer training seed. Early-only restart is
not a new proposal: upstream PR #27 and issue #16 predate this study [3, 4].
Figure 3. Generator budget fixed at 51,200 stories. The 9,600- and 19,200-step points are snapshots on one long, decaying
learning-rate schedule. The unconnected 4,800-step point is a separate run; the second long-run tokenizer scores 93.23 with
generator seed 42.
Longer training helps
At 38,400 steps, two tokenizer seeds give 91.46 and
93.23 (mean 92.35), 10.9% below the single 4,800-step
baseline of 103.61. Relative to 66.26 on the official
tokenizer, the ratio remains 1.39×. The official tokenizer
saw 12.5× more stories.
Reconstruction is an imperfect guide
Generation improves even as perfect reconstruction
falls. Across ten own tokenizer evaluations, code usage
has Spearman correlation −0.90 with PPL (−0.83
without two snapshots), versus −0.48 for perfect-story
reconstruction. This small, post-hoc association has
exceptions and does not replace a generator evaluation.

REMAINING GAP
Gianluca Meola  ·  Research note v0.1  ·  November 2026
4 A gap under longer generator training
This sweep uses the 2,400-step R12 tokenizer. It is a separate experiment from the 38,400-step result on the
previous page.
Figure 4. Both tokenizers are frozen. Two generator seeds at 51,200 and 409,600 stories; at 102,400, two on the official tokenizer and
one on R12. Separately, the authors’ full-budget model scores 16.58 here versus 15.41 in the paper (+7.6%, unexplained); those are
not matched-budget results.
Increasing generator exposure eightfold improves both models: 66.26 to 25.88 on the official tokenizer and
108.17 to 42.00 on R12. The ratio is 1.63×, 1.50× and 1.62× across the three budgets. This recipe and exposure
range do not close the gap for this tokenizer pair.

Worse in this setting; other normalisation

No material effect detected on two seeds at

Evidence narrows the search; it does not exclude whole causes
The 1.39× gap from the longer tokenizer has not received the same generator-budget sweep. Similar validation
cross-entropies across different tokenizers do not establish equal prediction quality, because their target code
distributions differ.

DIAGNOSTICS
Gianluca Meola  ·  Research note v0.1  ·  November 2026
5 Level 0: an observation, not a cause
The coarsest code plays different roles in reconstruction and in the generator’s conditioning.
Diagnostic
Official tokenizer
Tokenizer trained here
Decoded tokens changed by an L0 swap
4.0–5.5% in R12 batch-256 tokenizers
at 4,800+ steps
Generator loss rise after an L0 swap
About +0.25 to +0.29 nats in tested
models
Extra token errors: 10% corruption, levels 1–11
The official decoder is nearly insensitive to swapping level 0, yet the generator relies on that code: its loss rises
when level 0 comes from a different story. In several tokenizers trained here, the decoder is more sensitive. This
makes the role of level 0 a useful open question, not a demonstrated explanation of the PPL gap.
A counterexample matters
The tokenizer trained at batch 4,096 also has an almost inert level 0: only 0.05% of decoded tokens change when
it is swapped. Its Gen. PPL is still 100.36. An inert level 0 alone is therefore insufficient to reproduce the official
tokenizer’s result.

Random code substitutions probe decoder sensitivity; they do not reproduce the generator’s actual error distribution. Similar
aggregate damage at levels 1–11 cannot rule out per-level effects or correlated prediction errors.

DISCUSSION & ARTIFACTS
Gianluca Meola  ·  Research note v0.1  ·  November 2026
6 What the study supports
A practical training record with measurable gains; the full-budget explanation remains open.
Supported conclusions
Data-based codebook initialisation is a strong
improvement in the tested short-budget comparison.
The generator learns substantially faster with the
retuned short-run recipe. Extending tokenizer
training improves downstream PPL, but does not
match the official tokenizer.
Short generator runs can reveal a large difference
between a fixed pair of tokenizers. They are less
reliable for nearby choices: the 4,800- versus
2,400-step ranking reverses when generator exposure
increases from 51,200 to 102,400 stories, with
differences within the study’s noise thresholds.
Limits and next discriminating tests
The evidence covers one small English dataset, short
sequences, few training seeds and one automatic
text-quality metric. It does not establish competitive
general language ability, a new state of the art, or full
reproduction of the original NCM result.
The next useful controls are a generator-budget
sweep on the 38,400-step tokenizer, an independent
tokenizer seed for the isolated restart effect, and
longer tokenizer training with matched batch and
schedule choices. A decoder-inert level 0 is a possible
experiment, not a validated remedy.

Weights: huggingface.co/janlu89/ncm-12gb. Mean results in the figures must not be confused with individual
checkpoint scores. Different tokenizer checkpoints learn different code spaces and are not interchangeable for a fixed
generator.
Measured resource use
On an RTX 3080 Ti, a 51,200-story generator run takes roughly 10–12 minutes and peaks at 7.0 GiB allocated by
PyTorch; 409,600 stories take 62–70 minutes. A 38,400-step tokenizer takes about 3 h 15 min. Host: Intel i5-6600K,
Windows 10, PyTorch 2.14.1 / CUDA 12.6. These are local timings for the specified configurations, not a total
project-cost estimate.

Training checkpoints support pause and resume. A deterministic short test matches uninterrupted training exactly; the

rerun or overwrite model weights when building this document.
